extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 6, the first issue after the scene date. New to the corpus: the Chicago Reading Room raising a joint-stock company for premises, a lot sale quoting block numbers and Dearborn Street frontages in feet, J. Wright selling oak scantling, Wm. Sabine selling lumber waggons, and a stray horse eight miles up the North Branch. It also confirms three placements the run had half of: the auction room is at David Carver's old stand, Henry Moore's office is in J. H. Kinzie's new STORE, and the Tremont House is where the Reading Room's directors meet.

A meeting of the board of directors of the [Chi]cago Reading Room, held at the Tremont [Ho]use on Monday evening, July 6th, for the pur[pose] of consulting upo[n] mean[s] for ob[t]aining [a buil]ding suitable for the Read[in]g Ro[o]m, the fol[low]ing preamble and resolutions were adopted. claims.notes: A BUILDING THE TOWN WANTS AND DOES NOT HAVE, five days after the scene date — which makes it a negative claim of exactly the useful kind. The Chicago Reading Room exists as an institution with a BOARD OF DIRECTORS, and it is meeting to work out how to get premises, costed at $2,500 to $3,000 raised by joint stock. So on 1835-07-01 there is no reading-room building, and the directors meet in a hotel. IT ALSO CORROBORATES THE TREMONT HOUSE a second time and independently of Tuthill King's placement: a hotel with a room the town's directors sit in on a Monday evening. The secretary is Henry Moore, the attorney whose office this same issue puts in J. H. Kinzie's new store.

claims.notes: PLAT-GRAIN EVIDENCE, WHICH THIS CORPUS HAS ALMOST NONE OF: named lots in named blocks with FRONTAGES IN FEET — 45 feet on Dearborn Street and 90 feet deep, on a sub-division of lots 5 and 6. Those are dimensions this project's parcel work can be checked against directly. WHAT IS BROKEN AND WHY IT IS STILL RECORDED: the block numbers survive unevenly (16, 9[3], [8]4) and the column edge takes the second street name ('aiph street', where 'Ralph' is not a Chicago street and the fragment is more likely the tail of another word), so no single lot here can be resolved to a corner. The claim is the MEASUREMENTS and the fact that some of these lots already carry buildings — 'Some of the [buil]dings upon them' — which is a statement about the built density of the platted blocks in July 1835. Signed G. S. Hubbard, the same man the railroad commission names two issues earlier.

claims.notes: OAK SCANTLING FOR SALE IN CHICAGO, JULY 1835 — structural timber, sized and sold by the foot, which is the most directly usable building-material claim in the run. This project frames buildings and has been reasoning about member sizes from practice rather than from a Chicago advertisement; here is one. The quantity is cut before 'FEET' and is not supplied. J. WRIGHT is the same name the auction room places itself east of on South Water Street (1835-06-27, 07-04), and the street is recorded on his ENTITY on that reasoning while the business placement is left `none`, because an anchor someone else gives you is weaker evidence than an address you print yourself. Philo Carpenter's boots and clothing lines are quoted in the same spans: a druggist who also sells brogans and clothing, which is worth knowing before his trade is treated as narrow.

claims.notes: VEHICLES, NAMED BY TYPE, FOR SALE ON A CHICAGO WHARF STREET: LUMBER WAGGONS and ONE HORSE PLEASURE carriages. This project puts wagons in its streets and has had to choose their kind from period practice; this is the town's own forwarding merchant advertising which kinds were actually to be had here in July 1835, and the distinction between a working lumber waggon and a one-horse pleasure carriage is exactly the one a street dressing has to make. The word between them is destroyed and is not guessed at. Old Monongahela whiskey in the same column is the same merchant's stock.

That is a WAREHOUSE-SCALE stock and it is what a forwarding house on the river was holding a fortnight after the scene date; the units on the first two figures are cut ('do.' referring back to a line the segmenter destroyed) and are NOT supplied, so only the barrels of lard carry their unit. Useful to this project as a statement about what the riverside storehouses were full of.

claims.notes: A SETTLER PLACED OUTSIDE THE TOWN BY HIS OWN NOTICE: John K. Clark, EIGHT MILES UP THE NORTH BRANCH, advertising a stray horse in July 1835. This project's scene stops at the town and its immediate ground; a documented name and distance up the north branch is the kind of thing that tells it what the country beyond the edge of the model actually held, and estray notices are the only class of advertisement that routinely gives a rural address. TWO OTHER NOTICES ARE IN THE SAME SPAN and are quoted with it because the segmenter runs them together: Brackett's Dearborn Street wine store, and the lease notice which now finishes the sentence 1835-07-04 could only half-read — inquiries go to 'the office of He[nry Moore], J. H. Kinzie's new STORE', which is the word that was cut in Moore's own card ('J. H. Kinzie's New lon'). So Kinzie's new building is a store with a lawyer's office in it.

The definite article matters: it says the second half of the corner is not a plain street name but something taking 'the', which is why none of the plat's cross streets has been substituted in any of the three claims. Lake Street is documented in two of three printings and is recorded; the rest stays inside `[uncertain: …]`.

claims.notes: THE PORT COLUMN FOR THE WEEK AFTER THE SCENE DATE, and the pattern the run has been building holds: the same four or five hulls — Philips, Llewelling, Swan, Whig, St. Joseph, the brig Neptune — working a short circuit between Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Joseph and Buffalo. That is the traffic a reconstruction of the river mouth should be dressing for: not many ships, the SAME ships, several times a month. The dates are stripped out of this printing's arrivals list by the segmenter and are not reconstructed from the week's calendar.

claims.notes: THE POST OFFICE'S RULES, EXPANDED A WEEK AFTER THE FIRST NOTICE, and the new sentence is the human one: people are collecting letters FOR THEIR FRIENDS at the mail opening, and the postmaster now wants written orders so the delivery can be entered accurately. That is a crowd at a counter, which is how a reconstruction should picture the building. Sunday opening is here extended to an hour and a half against the previous notice's one hour. Signed by Hogan again; the initials are cut to 'S. C.' in this printing and the full form is carried by 1835-07-04's.
